processing: Details are not well documented. It is filed here as ripe pu-erh, which would mean wet-piled fermentation of Yunnan sun-dried tea; the name suggests fine, tippy leaf.
harvest_season: Not documented for this tea. Ripe teas are usually made from stored material rather than one picking.
appearance_dry: Not well documented; the name, White Needle Golden Lotus, suggests fine tippy leaf, and ripe teas of this kind are usually golden-tipped and brown.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft brown leaf, as typical of fine ripe pu-erh.
taste_profile: No dependable tasting notes exist for this tea. High-grade ripe pu-erh is typically smooth and sweet, with less earth than coarse blends.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for fine-leaf ripe tea: rinse quickly and keep early steeps short, because small leaf gives up colour fast.

vintage_note: How this tea is sold is poorly documented. Ripe pu-erh is usually sold by production year and batch, so ask for both. Check the characters closely, since the similarly named Jin Zhen Bai Lian from Dayi is far more common on the market.
description:
Bai Zhen Jin Lian, literally White Needle Golden Lotus, is listed in the tea glossary Babelcarp as a high-grade pu-erh made by the Menghai company, at least. That is nearly all that can be said with confidence, and the entry does not say whether it is ripe or raw.

It is filed here as ripe. If it follows other high-grade Menghai ripe teas, expect small tippy leaf and a smooth cup rather than a coarse, woody one.

Brew it as you would any fine ripe tea, with a quick rinse and short early steeps.

The practical trap is the name. Dayi sells a ripe tea called Jin Zhen Bai Lian, Golden Needle White Lotus, with almost the same words in another order. Read the wrapper and do not assume the two are one tea.
history: Little is documented about this tea beyond its name and its attribution to Menghai. No firm date of creation or account of its makers has been established.
